passage: "Pooja, you know, when I was your age there were no phones, but there was the TV. I watched every serial, even the late ones. I stopped playing badminton with my friends. My eyes were always tired in class. One day I fell asleep during a test and my teacher woke me. I was so ashamed. After that, my father made a rule: TV off at nine, and one evening a week in the park, no excuses. I grumbled for a month. Then I noticed I felt better and my marks went up." Gargi Maasi nudged the phone on the table. "So what's your rule going to be?"

qa.q: What happened during Gargi's test?
qa.a: She fell asleep during a test and her teacher woke her.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel when her teacher woke her?
qa.a: She felt ashamed about falling asleep.

qa.q: What could Pooja try to balance screen time?
qa.a: Pooja could set a switch-off time and plan outdoor play on some evenings, like Gargi's rule.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Pooja's own phone use after this story?
qa.a: Pooja may start to notice how screens affect sleep and schoolwork.

grounding: An elder tells a story about balancing screens with sleep, study and outdoor play.

passage: It had rained for five days straight, and Jatin hadn't been outside once. He'd been playing the racing game since morning. Sonali saw his homework untouched and his eyes red. "Jatin, game off after this race." He groaned. "But I can't go out anyway!" She thought. "Okay. Homework first. Then one hour of game. Then we play carrom." After dinner, Jatin beat her at carrom and forgot about the game. At nine, he put the tablet in the kitchen drawer himself.

qa.q: Where did Jatin put the tablet at nine?
qa.a: He put it in the kitchen drawer himself.

qa.q: What does Jatin's groan suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was frustrated about stopping and felt stuck indoors.

qa.q: What plan did Sonali make to balance Jatin's day?
qa.a: Homework first, then one hour of the game, then carrom together.

qa.q: How might Jatin see the rainy day differently after carrom?
qa.a: He may see there are fun things besides games, even when he can't go outside.

grounding: It shows a child balancing gaming with homework, play and sleep during bad weather.

passage: In their Siliguri flat, Jyoti was stuck on level twelve of her phone game at ten at night. Her eyes stung. The doorbell rang in the morning: it was Tenzin. "Football in the park?" Jyoti yawned. "I'm so tired." "Were you gaming again?" She nodded. On the way to the park, she said, "I'm putting an alarm for nine. Game off, bed." That evening the alarm rang. She paused, groaned, and turned it off. The next morning she scored two goals.

qa.q: Which level was Jyoti stuck on?
qa.a: She was stuck on level twelve.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's yawn and "I'm so tired" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the late-night gaming had left her without enough sleep.

qa.q: What small step did Jyoti take to fix her habit?
qa.a: She set an alarm for nine to stop gaming and go to bed.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel about Jyoti's change?
qa.a: Tenzin might be glad to have an energetic friend for football again.

grounding: It shows a child balancing gaming with outdoor play and sleep.

passage: 'Aparna, it's nine thirty.' 'One more level, Papa. Just one.' 'You said that at nine.' 'This one is different, the boss is almost dead!' Akash sat on the edge of her bed. 'How did you sleep last night?' Aparna rubbed her eyes. 'Bad. I kept dreaming about the castle.' 'And cycling with Reshma today?' 'Didn't go. I was playing.' She looked at the controller, then at him. 'Okay, can we make a deal? Games only after homework, and only till eight?' 'Deal. And the tablet sleeps in the hall.' 'Can I at least save first?' He smiled. 'Save, then goodnight.' She pressed save and yawned hugely. 'The boss will still be there tomorrow.'

qa.q: Where did Papa say the tablet would sleep?
qa.a: He said the tablet would sleep in the hall.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel about her gaming by the end of the talk?
qa.a: She seemed a little guilty and ready to change: she admitted she slept badly, dreamed about the game and skipped cycling, then suggested a deal herself.

qa.q: What made Papa's approach work?
qa.a: He asked about her sleep and missed cycling instead of scolding, and let her help set the rule and save the game.

qa.q: How might Reshma feel if Aparna keeps the deal?
qa.a: She would probably be glad to have her cycling friend back in the evenings.

grounding: Shows a child balancing gaming with homework, outdoor play and sleep through a family agreement.

passage: Last summer I played my phone game every night until my eyes burned. I'm twelve, so I thought I could handle it. Then one morning I fell asleep in the maths period and Sir had to tap my desk and say, 'Ujjwal, wake up.' Everyone laughed. Worse, Kishore stopped calling me for cricket because I always said 'later'. One evening I saw the boys playing from the balcony and felt left out, even though it was my own fault. So I made myself a rule: homework first, then cricket till dark, then one hour of games, and the phone goes to Amma at ten. The first week was hard. Now I sleep better and I bowl better too.

qa.q: What happened to Ujjwal in the maths period?
qa.a: Ujjwal fell asleep and Sir had to tap the desk while everyone laughed.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal feel while watching the boys playing from the balcony?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt left out, and a bit guilty, knowing the late-night gaming had caused the distance from cricket.

qa.q: What was good about the rule Ujjwal made?
qa.a: It still kept games in Ujjwal's day but put homework, outdoor play and sleep first, so it was realistic to follow.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the change in Ujjwal?
qa.a: Kishore would likely be happy to have a friend back on the field and less annoyed by hearing 'later' every time.

grounding: Illustrates a child learning to balance screen games with homework, outdoor play and sleep.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 6. Vijay Kulkarni.
For two weeks Vaibhav (eleven) yawned through first period and twice fell asleep during reading. His homework was half-done.
I asked him quietly at break. He said he played a football game on his phone in bed “until the battery dies.” He looked embarrassed.
I didn't scold him. I called his parents. Together with Vaibhav, they agreed: the phone charges in the kitchen at night; games only after homework and after playing outside.
This week Vaibhav was awake in first period and scored his best in the spelling test. He told me he now plays real football in the evenings.
Next step: a class talk on sleep and screens.

qa.q: Where does the phone charge at night now?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he told the teacher about the phone?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about playing until the battery died.

qa.q: Why was including Vaibhav in the agreement a good idea?
qa.a: He helped make the plan, so he was more likely to follow it.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's parents feel after seeing the change?
qa.a: They are probably relieved and pleased that he is sleeping better and playing outside.

grounding: A teacher notes an eleven-year-old balancing games with sleep, homework and outdoor play.

passage:
Friday
After school I wanted to play my racing game. Sarita-didi said, “Homework first, then the lane, then game.” I groaned.
But Rohan and Faiz were already playing cricket outside. I did my maths fast and ran down.
We played till the streetlights came on. I hit two fours!
Then I played the game for a bit. When Amma called for dinner, I actually didn't mind stopping. And after dinner I was so tired I fell asleep reading.
Maybe didi is right. My eyes don't hurt tonight. — Sahil

qa.q: What did Sahil hit in cricket?
qa.a: Two fours.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Sahil felt happy and tired, not minding stopping the game, with eyes that didn't hurt.

qa.q: What routine helped Sahil balance the day?
qa.a: Homework first, then outdoor play, then a little game time before dinner and sleep.

qa.q: How might Sarita-didi feel reading Sahil's diary?
qa.a: Sarita-didi would probably be pleased and a bit amused that the advice worked.

grounding: A ten-year-old balances homework, outdoor play, a game and sleep.

passage:
In their village above Namchi, Pema, nine, came home from school and reached for her mother's phone to watch videos.
Charu, her neighbour and best friend, shouted from the gate. “Pema! Kite on the hill!”
Pema hesitated. “Mama said I can have the phone after homework anyway.”
“So do homework, kite, then phone.”
They did their sums on the steps together. Then they flew the red kite until the fog rolled in. Pema watched two short videos before dinner.
That night she fell asleep before nine, a smudge of kite string still on her fingers.

qa.q: What colour was the kite?
qa.a: The kite was red.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when Charu called about the kite?
qa.a: She felt torn between the videos and flying the kite.

qa.q: What plan helped Pema balance her afternoon?
qa.a: Doing homework first, then flying the kite, then watching two short videos.

qa.q: How does Charu help Pema?
qa.a: Charu invites her to play outside and suggests an order that fits everything in.

grounding: A nine-year-old balances videos with homework, outdoor play and sleep.

passage:
In their flat in Istanbul, Elif played her racing game under the blanket until almost midnight. The next morning she yawned through maths and missed an easy question. At football, she tripped twice.
Her brother Sami found her dozing on the sofa after school. "You're a zombie."
"I'm fine," she mumbled.
That evening, the new level unlocked. Elif's thumb hovered over the button. She looked at her bag, still packed with homework, and at the football by the door.
She put the tablet on the kitchen shelf. "Sami, don't let me take it to bed."
"Deal," said Sami. "Want to kick the ball first?"

qa.q: Where did Elif put the tablet?
qa.a: On the kitchen shelf.

qa.q: What was Elif feeling when her thumb hovered over the button?
qa.a: Elif felt tempted and torn between the new level and her homework and football.

qa.q: Which choice helped Elif, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the tablet in the kitchen at night took away the temptation, so she could sleep and do her homework.

qa.q: How does Sami see Elif's tiredness?
qa.a: Sami notices she's like a "zombie" and supports her plan by agreeing not to let her take the tablet to bed.

grounding: A child in Turkey notices late-night gaming is hurting her day and sets a limit.

passage:
At the school hostel, lights-out was at nine. Hansa lay under her blanket watching funny videos on her phone, the screen lighting up her face.
At eleven, Jagdish Sir, the warden, knocked softly and shone his torch. "Phone, please."
Hansa handed it over, cheeks hot.
The next morning she fell asleep in the library. At kabaddi practice she was slow.
That evening, Jagdish Sir sat with her in the common room. "Games and videos are fine. But sleep is when your body grows and your brain sorts the day. What if you watch after dinner, and I keep the phone at night?"
Hansa thought, then nodded. "Only after dinner."

qa.q: What time was lights-out at the hostel?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she handed over the phone?
qa.a: Hansa felt embarrassed at being caught.

qa.q: What plan did Jagdish Sir suggest, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: He suggested watching after dinner and keeping the phone at night, which keeps fun time but protects sleep.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Sir feel when Hansa agrees?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir probably feels relieved that she accepted a fair plan instead of arguing.

grounding: A hostel warden helps a child balance videos with sleep and activity.

passage:
I'm Karthik, Sangeeta's brother. Last summer, she was stuck on a farming game on Amma's phone. Every morning she'd grab it before brushing her teeth.
Then the colony boys started a cricket match in the evenings. The first day she said no. The second day she watched from the balcony, the phone still in her hand.
On the third day she left the phone on the charger and came down. She was a terrible bowler. But she came back sweaty and laughing, and slept early.
After that, she played her game only in the afternoon. I don't know if she planned it, but it seemed to work.

qa.q: What game was Sangeeta stuck on?
qa.a: A farming game.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been feeling when she watched from the balcony?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably felt curious and tempted to join, but still pulled by the game.

qa.q: What could help Sangeeta keep the balance she found?
qa.a: Keeping her game time to the afternoon and making sure evenings stay for outdoor play.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Sangeeta's change?
qa.a: Karthik isn't sure if she planned it, but sees her play outside, sleep earlier and use the game less.

grounding: A sibling watches a child shift from a phone game to outdoor play and better sleep.

passage:
Monday: Gautam, ten, played a racing game on his phone until midnight. At school he fell asleep in maths. His friend Devika poked him awake.
Wednesday: His mother made a deal: games only after homework, one hour, phone charges in the kitchen at nine. Gautam grumbled and slammed his door.
Saturday: Devika called him to the park for cricket. He went, and they played until dark. That night he slept by ten without meaning to. "Cricket's better than the racing game," he admitted to Devika. "Don't tell my mum."

qa.q: Where does the phone charge at nine?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when his mother made the deal?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and resentful, grumbling and slamming his door.

qa.q: What helped Gautam balance games with play and sleep?
qa.a: Clear limits at home and a friend inviting him to play outside.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when Gautam says cricket is better?
qa.a: Devika likely feels happy and a little triumphant.

grounding: Tracks a child balancing gaming with outdoor play and sleep.

passage:
Kalyani, you ask why I don't let your little brother play games at night? Let me tell you about me during one summer vacation, when I was eleven.
I, Jahnavi, got a hand-held game from my uncle. I played it day and night. I stopped going to the river with my friends. I got headaches. I became cranky with everyone.
One evening my grandmother took the game and put it in her cupboard. I cried and cried.
The next day, bored, I went to the river. My friends had built a raft. I'd missed it.
After that, I played the game one hour after lunch, and spent evenings outside. Summers are too short for screens only.

qa.q: What had Jahnavi's friends built?
qa.a: A raft.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when the grandmother took the game?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt upset and angry, crying and crying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jahnavi's story?
qa.a: Going to the river the next day and seeing what had been missed, then choosing one hour of games and evenings outside.

qa.q: How might the grandmother have felt taking the game?
qa.a: She likely felt worried about the headaches and firm but caring.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a child to balance gaming with outdoor play.

passage:
The night before his Class 6 exam, Dhruv, eleven, was stuck on a game level. Just one more try. His cousin Vishal, staying for the Holi holidays, said, "It's eleven. Exam's at eight."
"One more!"
Vishal waited. Dhruv lost again. And again.
At midnight, Vishal took the phone gently. "Sleep. The level will still be there."
Dhruv argued, then flopped on his bed. He slept badly and woke tired.
In the exam he yawned through the first page. On the way home he said, "I should've stopped at eleven."
Vishal said, "Next time, you stop it yourself."

qa.q: What time was Dhruv's exam?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel during the exam?
qa.a: He felt tired and regretful, yawning through the first page.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do differently next time?
qa.a: Set a stop time before exams and put the phone away himself.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel about taking the phone?
qa.a: Vishal probably felt uncomfortable but caring, wanting Dhruv to do well.

grounding: Shows a child learning the cost of late gaming before an exam.

passage:
On the second night of the Christmas holidays, Thomas, ten, was still gaming at midnight in his Bengaluru flat, headphones on. The next morning he slept through breakfast and snapped at his mother. By afternoon his eyes felt gritty.
His friend Gurleen rang the bell at four. "Cricket in the park? We need one more."
"I'm on level twelve," Thomas said. Then he looked out at the sun and the other kids. He saved the game.
He played till dark and came home starving, cheeks red.
That night he told his mother, "Maybe one hour of games after homework, and the tablet sleeps in the hall." She smiled. "Your idea. I like it."
He was asleep by ten.

qa.q: Where does the tablet sleep in Thomas's new plan?
qa.a: The tablet sleeps in the hall.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling the morning after gaming till midnight?
qa.a: He felt tired and irritable, sleeping through breakfast and snapping at his mother.

qa.q: What small step helped Thomas balance screens with play and sleep?
qa.a: Saying yes to cricket, then suggesting his own one-hour limit with the tablet kept out of his room.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when Thomas comes to play?
qa.a: Gurleen would probably feel happy and relieved, since they needed one more player and Thomas joined in.

grounding: Shows a child noticing how late gaming affects him and choosing a better balance with outdoor play and sleep.
